episodes.title: Viral
episodes.borrowed: The live stream that goes huge while Anton overheats in the garage and the team scrambles to keep it alive

cold_open.say: Everybody up. Everybody. A chef with nine million followers just posted about us.
She says Forkcast found her a table in thirty seconds. We've had four thousand sign-ups since dinner.
Why is the garage making that noise?
Because Forkcast lives in the garage now. I moved it to Aleister last night.
We were paying for hosting.
We were paying a stranger to do my job badly. Aleister is fine. He's just warm.
He's warm like a toaster is warm. That's a desk fan, Gilroy.
Yes, hello, Ulrich Bachner. The incubator. Did I see it coming? I designed it coming.
I'm going to be sick.

brief.say: She's posting again tomorrow at eight, in the Friday dinner rush, to people who'll be awake this time.
The garage won't make it to eight. I say that with love.
Good news! I've written a plan. It's called Make Forkcast Web-Scale. I'm very proud of it.

cards.label: Move to the cloud
cards.plain: Rent an app server and a managed Postgres database, and move Forkcast out of the garage.

takes.say: You'd be paying someone to babysit a server I already babysit.
Gilroy, the server is on fire. A little bit. In places.

cards.label: Kubernetes
cards.plain: Split Forkcast into twelve small services running on a container cluster.

takes.say: It's how Hubbub does it. If we're going to do it, we should do it right.
Twelve things to break instead of one, for a team of five. Bold.

cards.label: Add a cache
cards.plain: Keep copies of recent answers in Redis so the database isn't asked the same thing over and over. I've set everything to one hour!

takes.say: Caches make everything faster. That's just science.
A cache is a machine for telling people things that used to be true.

cards.label: CDN for photos
cards.plain: Serve photos and scripts from servers near each diner instead of from our app.

takes.say: Every page has fourteen photos of risotto. Get them off our server.
And when a restaurant changes its photos? Oh, they can be an hour old. Lovely.

cards.label: Queue sign-up work
cards.plain: Put welcome emails and other sign-up chores in a queue, and let a worker get through them.

takes.say: Each sign-up waits while we send its welcome email. Fifteen thousand at once is a lot of waiting.
Nobody needs their welcome email this exact second.

cards.label: Rewrite in Rust
cards.plain: Rewrite the booking code in Rust. Rust is very fast!

takes.say: Serious companies rewrite in Rust. It's practically a funding round.
The app isn't slow. It's waiting for the database. You'd be speeding up the waiting.

cards.label: Forty servers
cards.plain: Forty app servers. Small ones, but forty.

takes.say: Hubbub has forty thousand servers. Forty is the least we can do. More servers, more fast.
Ulrich, every one of those talks to the same database, and the database can only...

cards.label: Add an index
cards.plain: Add an index on bookings by restaurant and night, so finding tonight's tables doesn't read every booking.

takes.say: Like the index in a book. Thirty minutes of work.
Boring. Correct. My favourite combination.

cards.label: Cache AI answers
cards.plain: Answer popular questions from a cache, and use prompt caching so the long fixed start of each prompt is billed at a fraction.

takes.say: Half our searches are 'date night in the Mission'. We shouldn't pay for that answer twice.
The answers can be an hour old. Restaurants don't move.

cards.label: Shard by city
cards.plain: Split the database into one per city. Very web-scale!

takes.say: We're in one city, but we could be in more cities! Later!
I've seen a sharding project before. I was much younger when it started.

cards.label: Biggest AI model
cards.plain: Switch the concierge to the biggest model there is.

takes.say: Five times the price per answer, but five times the... vibes?
The answers were fine. The bill was the problem.

reply.say: I measured last night. The database was at a hundred percent, almost all of it on 'free tables near me tonight'.
It reads every booking we've ever had. Every time. We need an index.
Menus and photos change about once a day. An hour old is fine.
Tonight's free tables change every couple of minutes. An hour old is a lie.
And 'My bookings' is different for every person.

asks.text: Is this cache per user or shared?

reply.say: Shared! Everyone gets the same copy. Of everything. Including 'My bookings'.
Oh.
That happened at a company I used to work for. Everyone saw everyone's bookings. I still dream about it.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: The model calls are four fifths of the bill. And the provider caps how many we can make a minute.
I can cache AI answers! I should have thought of that.
Web-scale! My favourite. I'll shard the database by city!
The smartest one! Diners will feel the difference. Your accountant will too.

hotfixes.label: Add another app server
hotfixes.say: Traffic just doubled! Hotfix: add another app server? It's {monthly} a month.

corner.say: Aleister is down. Get the other fan. GET THE OTHER FAN.
The app servers are maxed out. Is that bad? That's bad.
The database is reading every booking again. And again.
People keep picking tables that went a minute ago.
A diner in Oakland can see someone's anniversary booking. This is the dream again.
Why does everyone keep getting logged out?
Forty servers, one database, a hundred connections. Do the maths, Ulrich.
The model provider is turning our searches away.
Fifteen thousand sign-ups, all waiting on welcome emails.
We're serving every risotto photo ourselves.
Twelve thousand users. TWELVE. I'm texting everyone I know.

garage_melt.title: Aleister overheated and shut down.
garage_melt.plain: One server in a garage ran the app and the database together. Past its limit it got hot, switched itself off, and Forkcast went with it.

full_scan.title: The database read every booking ever made, every time.
full_scan.plain: Finding tonight's free tables meant reading the whole bookings table, and every new booking made the next search longer.
full_scan.term: a full table scan; the fix is an index
full_scan.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add an index for this query.

no_cache.title: The database answered the same menu questions thousands of times.
no_cache.plain: Menus barely change, but every page asked the database for them again.
no_cache.tell_ai: Cache this. How stale can it be?

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Add a server, and make the servers stateless.

no_cdn.title: Our own servers were sending every photo.
no_cdn.plain: Photos and scripts are most of what a page weighs, and our app was serving all of them.
no_cdn.tell_ai: Serve static files from a CDN.

no_queue.title: Fifteen thousand sign-ups hit the app at once.
no_queue.plain: Every sign-up held a server while it sent the welcome email, a slow call to an email service. That could have waited in a line.
no_queue.tell_ai: Put work that can wait on a queue.

stale_tables.title: Diners booked tables that were already taken.
stale_tables.plain: The cache kept tonight's tables too long. They change every couple of minutes, so diners kept picking tables that had gone.

cache_leak.title: Diners saw other people's bookings.
cache_leak.plain: 'My bookings' went into a shared cache, so one diner's page was handed to everyone who came next. That's a data breach.
cache_leak.term: per-user data in a shared cache
cache_leak.tell_ai: Is this cache per user or shared?

stateless.title: Diners kept getting logged out.
stateless.plain: Each server remembered logins in its own memory. With more than one server, the next request often landed on one that had never met you.
stateless.tell_ai: Make the servers stateless: keep sessions in Redis.

too_many_connections.title: Most servers couldn't reach the database.
too_many_connections.plain: Every server holds ten connections to the database, and our Postgres allows a hundred. Forty servers wanted four hundred.
too_many_connections.term: the connection limit; a connection pooler shares them
too_many_connections.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls you can make a minute. Past the cap, searches failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

ai_bill.title: The AI bill hit five figures in one night.
ai_bill.plain: Every search paid for a fresh answer, even the thousandth 'date night in the Mission'.
ai_bill.tell_ai: Cache AI answers, and use prompt caching.

big_model.title: The biggest model cost five times as much.
big_model.plain: The answers didn't need it. The bill noticed.
big_model.tell_ai: What's the simplest version that works?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

lessons.plain: A nearby copy of an answer, so you don't work it out again. Ask how stale it can be, and whose it is: per-user data is cached per user, never shared.
Find the bottleneck first. Then a bigger server, or more servers behind a load balancer, kept stateless so any of them can take any request. Most apps never need much more.

lines.say: Fifty thousand users! I want to see them. All of them. On a screen. Updating every hour.
In the boardroom. By Monday. Make it huge.
On... which database?

episodes.title: The Board Meeting
episodes.borrowed: Richard pushed out as CEO by the board, and Jack Barker's box

cold_open.say: Fifty thousand users! Where's my screen? I said a screen. I said huge.
We've voted. Forkcast needs an experienced CEO.
This is Mack Barlow. He's run three companies.
Four. One was a boat. Love the energy in this room. Love the little app.
As a board member, I voted for Mack. As your mentor, I voted with a heavy heart. Both were yes.
You stay on as Head of Product. You keep the robot. I'll handle the vision.
What... is the vision?
Two things. A dashboard on every screen in this building, live. And a box.
A box.
People can hold a box.

brief.say: The board comes back Friday night to watch the dinner rush on the big screen. With prospects. Box prospects.
A normal busy Friday: fifteen thousand diners at the peak. Bookings have to keep working while the board watches.
I've written a plan! It's called Dashboards For Everyone. Every number, live, every minute!

cards.label: Board dashboard
cards.plain: Forty live tiles on the boardroom screen and the board's laptops, straight from our database, refreshing every minute!

takes.say: Forty tiles! Can it be forty-one? Is forty-one bigger?
Every tile is a question for the database. Every screen, every minute. I'm only asking.

cards.label: Biggest database
cards.plain: Move Postgres to the biggest size there is: eight times the power, for eight times the price.

takes.say: Bigger is faster. I don't see the debate.
It'd work. It's also thirty-two hundred dollars a month, every month, for a screen.

cards.label: Read replica
cards.plain: A live copy of the database just for the dashboard, so its questions don't slow down bookings.

takes.say: A replica keeps the dashboard off the bookings. That part's real.
It's a copy of the same kind of database. Same huge questions, same slow answers, now in a second place.

cards.label: The Box
cards.plain: Sell every restaurant a Forkcast server for its back office. Hardware! Margins! A box!

takes.say: Investors understand boxes. You can hold a box. You can't hold a cloud.
We'd be fixing two hundred servers in two hundred restaurant basements. With our hands.

cards.label: Analytics DB
cards.plain: Copy the bookings every hour into a separate database built for big questions, and point the dashboard at that.

takes.say: You don't do the accounts at the front desk. At my last company the numbers had their own room. I had it painted.
I've checked it twice. He's right. Somebody write down the date.

cards.label: Error alerts
cards.plain: Track errors in the app and in every scheduled job, and message us the moment one fails.

takes.say: At a previous company we found out things were broken from the news.
Alerts are for people who write bugs.

cards.label: Real-time stream
cards.plain: Stream every booking into the analytics database the moment it happens, on a managed event-streaming cluster.

takes.say: Real time is the only time.
Chaz asked for hourly. That's three thousand a month for the other fifty-nine minutes.

cards.label: Two hundred tiles
cards.plain: Every number we have, on one enormous wall. Two hundred tiles!

takes.say: Now THAT is a dashboard.
Which of these numbers would change what we do?

asks.text: Is this OLTP or OLAP work?

reply.say: The app does lots of tiny jobs. Book this table, show my bookings. That's OLTP: the front desk.
Every tile asks a huge question across everything we've ever stored. That's OLAP: the accountant's office.
Two hundred and forty of those a minute, on the database that takes the bookings.

asks.text: How fresh do the numbers need to be?

reply.say: The board meets four times a year.
Chaz asked for every hour. An hour old is plenty for a board.

asks.text: How will we know if it breaks?

reply.say: Know? We'll... someone will mention it?
At a previous company we learned the payroll job had stopped when the pay stopped. I'd like alerts, please.
Alerts! Great idea. Mine now.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: The biggest database costs eight times as much, whatever the traffic. That's forever, not just Friday.
The dashboard asks the same questions at any traffic. More diners just means more rows to add up.
Real-time! I'll stream every booking as it happens. It's only a small cluster. Of servers. That we run.
Huge! Chaz's favourite word. Two hundred tiles, coming up!

events.banner: The board is watching the big screen

hotfixes.label: Fix and rerun the copy
hotfixes.say: Alert! The 8pm copy into the analytics database just failed: a restaurant put a noodle emoji in its name. Hotfix: handle it and rerun?

corner.say: Every time the board's screen refreshes, somebody's booking waits behind it.
Bookings are fine. The replica's drowning. The board's screen just says 'Loading'.
Two hundred tiles. The analytics database is turning them away.
Why does the big screen still say seven o'clock? Did we break time?
The screen says we've had nine bookings tonight. Nine. The prospects are looking at me.
The database is maxed out.
The app servers are maxed out. Is that bad? That's bad.
The model provider is turning our searches away.
Look at it go! Fifteen thousand! I'm screenshotting everything!

no_dashboard.title: There was no dashboard.
no_dashboard.plain: The board asked for one screen of numbers and got none. The bookings were fine; the board meeting wasn't.
no_dashboard.tell_ai: Build what the board asked for, as simply as it works.

olap_on_oltp.title: The board's dashboard slowed down the bookings.
olap_on_oltp.plain: Every tile asked a huge question across everything we've ever stored, again every minute, on the same database taking Friday's bookings. Bookings waited behind the board's questions.
olap_on_oltp.term: OLAP work on an OLTP database
olap_on_oltp.tell_ai: Is this OLTP or OLAP work? Put the analytics in a data warehouse.

replica_slow.title: The replica couldn't answer the dashboard.
replica_slow.plain: The copy kept the bookings safe, but it's the same kind of database, built for lots of small, quick questions. The dashboard's huge ones swamped it, and the board's screen timed out.
replica_slow.term: a read replica is still an OLTP database
replica_slow.tell_ai: Is this OLTP or OLAP work?

too_many_tiles.title: Two hundred tiles swamped the analytics database.
too_many_tiles.plain: Every tile is a question, and every screen asks it again every minute. Two hundred was more than our small analytics database could answer, and nobody could read them all anyway.
too_many_tiles.tell_ai: Show the few numbers that change a decision.

silent_failure.title: The 8pm copy job broke, and stayed broken.
silent_failure.plain: A restaurant's name broke the hourly copy into the analytics database. Nobody fixed it and ran it again, so the board's numbers stopped at 7pm and stayed there.
silent_failure.term: a failed pipeline job; alerts tell you, then someone fixes it
silent_failure.tell_ai: How will we know if it breaks? Add error tracking and alerts.

stale_numbers.title: The board watched last night's numbers.
stale_numbers.plain: The copy into the analytics database ran once a night, at 3am, so all Friday evening the big screen showed the morning's numbers.
stale_numbers.tell_ai: How fresh do the numbers need to be?

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Add a server, and make the servers stateless.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls you can make a minute. Past the cap, searches failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: What's the simplest version that works?

lessons.plain: The app's database is the front desk: lots of small, quick jobs. Big questions across everything go to a separate copy built for them, a data warehouse, kept up to date by copying new data across in regular batches.
Once it's live, you can't watch every screen and every job. Error tracking and alerts tell you something broke, ideally before your customers, or your board, do.

lines.say: Great news. Hubbub called. They loved the dashboard.
They asked a lot of questions about how Forkcast works. I answered all of them. In detail. With slides.
You what.
I'm going to be sick.

episodes.title: Hubbub Dine
episodes.borrowed: Hooli's Nucleus, the copycat built by hundreds of engineers, collapsing at its big launch, and Gavin Belson on stage with his spiritual adviser
episodes.place: Hubbub's campus, the keynote hall. Wednesday, 10am.

cold_open.say: Dinner. Humanity's oldest network. Hubbub has spent a year reimagining it.
Four hundred engineers. Two hundred and twelve microservices. One purpose: the table you deserve. Hubbub Dine.
That's Forkcast. That is literally Forkcast. His logo is a fork.
Friday at six, in the dinner rush, I'll book this whole hall a table, live, on stage. Smaller companies are welcome to watch.
Why does he know where all our restaurants are? Why does he know our NAME?
A man with silver hair and a boat gave him the slides on Saturday.
About that. The board let Mack go this morning. You're CEO again. Congratulations, I think.
And I've just had tea with Galen's spiritual adviser. Wonderful man. Barefoot, like me. He says we need microservices.
I brought a bag for Ricky. I bring a bag to everything now.

brief.say: Friday at six, a million people watch Galen's keynote with a dinner app open. Some of them will be trying ours.
Bookings have to work while the whole internet compares us with Hubbub Dine. Nineteen in twenty, not nine in ten.
I've written a plan! It's called Beat Hubbub Tonight. More servers! Every feature they have! It's going to be a bloodbath. A friendly one.

cards.label: More servers
cards.plain: Everyone will try both apps tonight, so more app servers behind the load balancer. I've set us to six: double!

takes.say: If Galen's audience all try us at once, I want spare servers. Spare everything.
How many is 'everyone'? Six is double the server bill for a night nobody's measured.

cards.label: Clone the clone
cards.plain: Copy every feature Hubbub Dine announced: voice booking, a loyalty scheme, and a table in the metaverse.

takes.say: They copied us, so we copy them copying us. It's basically poetry.
A company I used to work for copied every feature a rival had. Then the rival went out of business, and so did we.

cards.label: 8 services
cards.plain: Split Forkcast into eight services that call each other over the network, on a container cluster. Like Hubbub, but humble.

takes.say: Hubbub has two hundred and twelve. I'm asking for eight. That's humility. His adviser would weep.
Every arrow between them is a network call, and any call can fail. A booking would need eight of them to work.

cards.label: Rate limit API
cards.plain: Count each client's requests at the front door, and turn away anything over the limit with error 429. I've set a generous thousand a minute!

takes.say: Sixty machines. Each gets its fair share and not one request more. I find that beautiful.
Careful. Some diners tap through thirty restaurants in a minute. I'm one of them.

cards.label: Add CAPTCHAs
cards.plain: Make every diner prove they're human before each search and each booking. Bots hate it!

takes.say: Select every square with a fork in it!
People hate it too. Every puzzle is a moment to give up and try Hubbub Dine.

cards.label: Shard by city
cards.plain: Split the database into one per city. Web-scale, like last time!

takes.say: I kept the plan from last time. Just in case. I'm always just in case.
The database isn't tonight's problem. That would make it three databases that aren't the problem.

reply.say: Since the keynote, sixty machines in one cloud, each asking for tonight's tables about fifteen hundred times a minute. They call themselves HubbubBot.
They're copying every free table we have. That's how Hubbub Dine knows the city. On Friday they'll do it all night.
I could put a rate limit on our API! A limit for each client, at the front door.
Last Friday the app servers were at half their capacity at the peak, and the database at a tenth of its.
So three app servers carry about thirty thousand diners, and four about forty. If HubbubBot doesn't eat them first.
And if Hubbub Dine falls over on stage, its audience comes here. Call it thirty-five thousand at once.
Right now a booking is one app talking to one database.
Split it into eight services and a booking needs all eight to answer. If each answers ninety-nine calls in a hundred, all eight answer about ninety-two.
So about one booking in thirteen fails, somewhere, and somebody has to work out where.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: Each app server is a hundred and fifty a month. The cluster for microservices is four thousand.
And every request HubbubBot sends is one we pay to answer so that Hubbub can show it as theirs.
Bot-proof! A CAPTCHA before every search and every booking. Nobody gets dinner without finding the forks!
Web-scale again! You remembered! I'll shard the database by city!

events.banner: Hubbub Dine is live. So is HubbubBot
Hubbub Dine fell over on stage!

hotfixes.label: Add two app servers
hotfixes.say: Hubbub Dine just fell over on stage, and its diners are coming here! Hotfix: add two more app servers? It's {monthly} a month.

corner.say: HubbubBot is eating the app servers. We're paying to feed their app.
I just got a 429. Me. A human. I was choosing between two ramen places.
A booking failed somewhere between service four and service six. Nobody knows which. I'm making a spreadsheet.
People are failing the fork puzzle and booking with Hubbub instead. Well, they would be.
The app servers are maxed out. Is that bad? That's bad.
The database is maxed out.
The model provider is turning our searches away.
Hubbub's down and we're up! I'm texting Galen. I don't have his number. I'm texting everyone.

scraper.title: Hubbub's scraper swamped the app servers.
scraper.plain: Sixty of Hubbub's machines asked for tonight's tables about fifteen hundred times a minute each, and too much of that got through. Every request they sent was one our servers had to answer.
scraper.term: no rate limit, or one set too high
scraper.tell_ai: Rate limit our API, per client.

limit_too_tight.title: The rate limit turned away real diners.
limit_too_tight.plain: Ten requests a minute slowed HubbubBot to a trickle, and it stopped the diners who flick through restaurants quickly too. They got error 429 instead of dinner.
limit_too_tight.term: a rate limit set below what real users do
limit_too_tight.tell_ai: Set the limit well above what a busy person does.

service_chain.title: Bookings failed somewhere between the services.
service_chain.plain: A booking had to cross eight services, each a call over the network. Each worked ninety-nine times in a hundred, so all eight together worked about ninety-two times in a hundred.
service_chain.term: microservices: every call between them can fail
service_chain.tell_ai: Keep this one app until we measure a problem.

captcha.title: Diners gave up at the CAPTCHA.
captcha.plain: Every search and every booking asked diners to prove they were human first. Some couldn't, some wouldn't, and they went elsewhere.
captcha.term: a CAPTCHA's cost to real users
captcha.tell_ai: Rate limit the bots instead of puzzling the diners.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add a server.

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls you can make a minute. Past the cap, searches failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

lessons.plain: Cap how many requests each client can make a minute, and turn the rest away with error 429, so one greedy client can't use up the app for everyone else. Set the cap above what your busiest real users do, or it blocks them too.

Microservices split an app into small services that separate teams build and deploy on their own. The price is more moving parts: services call each other over the network, a long chain of calls adds delay, and the whole is harder to test. One app is simpler.

lines.say: Forty restaurants left Hubbub Dine last night and signed with us. They have one condition.
Deposits. Real money, taken through their own booking systems, so no-shows pay. By next Friday.
Money, moving between computers that don't trust each other, over a network. What could go wrong. Twice.
I'll get the bag.

episodes.title: Charged Twice
episodes.borrowed: PiperNet, the decentralised internet spread across thousands of phones, that works beautifully in a room and badly at scale
episodes.place: A trattoria in North Beach, the host stand. Monday, 6pm.

cold_open.say: This is one of the forty. The owner wants to see how deposits work before Friday. Be normal.
Their booking system is a beige box under the host stand. It has a fax modem. I respect it.
Good news first: HubbubBot stopped on Saturday. Hubbub Dine is 'pausing to reimagine'.
I haven't slept. I built something. Everybody, phones out, please. On the table.
ForkNet. Every phone keeps its own copy of tonight's tables and passes each booking to the phones nearby. No servers. Nothing in the middle to go down.
I booked table nine on mine, and it just showed up on Gerard's. Okay. That's actually beautiful.
Five phones. One room. One wifi. Friday is sixteen thousand phones on buses and in tunnels.
Decentralised. I've been saying that word for years, mostly at parties. I'll take my ten percent in ForkNet.
It worked every single time. I'm fine. I'm going to be fine.

brief.say: Friday the forty go live with deposits. Twenty dollars a head, taken when you book, kept if you don't show.
A normal busy Friday: sixteen thousand diners at the peak. Nobody pays twice, and nobody gets a table someone else already has.
I've written a plan! It's called Take Their Money. Working title. Payments can't fail now: I made them retry until they work!

cards.label: Take deposits
cards.plain: Take a deposit through the payment provider whenever someone books one of the forty. If the provider doesn't answer in time, I ask again until it does!

takes.say: Forty restaurants and real money. This is the business now.
Every deposit is a call to someone else's computer. Some of those calls won't come back. Some will come back late, which is worse.

cards.label: ForkNet
cards.plain: Run tonight's tables on the diners' phones: every phone keeps a copy and gossips each booking to the phones near it. No servers in the middle.

takes.say: It worked on all five phones, every time. Nothing in the middle means nothing in the middle can go down.
Every phone has its own copy, and the copies disagree until the gossip catches up. Two phones, one last table, both say yes.

cards.label: ForkCoin
cards.plain: Take deposits in our very own cryptocurrency instead of dollars! I've drafted the white paper. It's mostly diagrams.

takes.say: If we have a coin, I'm early. I have never once been early.

cards.label: Deposit IDs

cards.label: Hold the table

takes.say: Right now we check, wait a second and a half for the money, then book. Anyone can slip into that second and a half.
A company I used to work for booked two weddings into one hall. Both brides came. There was one cake.

cards.label: Backup provider

takes.say: Two providers! Twice the reliability! I think that's how maths works.

cards.label: Shard by city

asks.text: What if this is sent twice?

reply.say: Then I send it again! And again. Persistence is my best quality.
When a call times out, we don't know if it worked. Some of them did, and only the answer got lost. Retry those and the provider takes the deposit twice.
Unless every deposit carries its own key, the same one on every retry. Then the provider sees it's done that one already and just sends back the first answer.

asks.text: What if the provider is down?

reply.say: It won't be down. It'll be slow. Early on, one call in a hundred doesn't answer in time. In the rush, one in fifty. At the peak, one in seventeen.

I can hold the table first, in one transaction, and then take the money!

Never fail! If the provider doesn't answer, I'll take the deposit through a second one. Belt and braces!

no_deposits.title: There were no deposits.
no_deposits.plain: The forty restaurants signed on one condition, deposits, and we didn't take any. The night was quiet. So were the forty restaurants, afterwards.
no_deposits.tell_ai: Take deposits, as simply as it works.

double_charge.title: Diners were charged twice.
double_charge.plain: Some calls to the payment provider timed out after the deposit had gone through; only the answer was lost. We asked again, and the provider, seeing what looked like a new request, took the deposit again.
double_charge.tell_ai: What happens if this request is sent twice? Send an idempotency key.

timeout_unknown.title: Diners paid for tables we said they didn't get.
timeout_unknown.plain: When the provider didn't answer in time we told the diner the deposit had failed. For about half of them it hadn't: the money went through and only the answer was lost.
timeout_unknown.term: a timeout means you don't know
timeout_unknown.tell_ai: Retry with an idempotency key, so asking again is safe.

backup_provider.title: Diners were charged by both providers.
backup_provider.plain: When the first provider didn't answer in time, we took the deposit through the second. For about half of those, the first had already taken it. Our numbers mean nothing to a different company.
backup_provider.tell_ai: What happens if this request is sent twice?

double_booking.title: Two parties got the same table.
double_booking.plain: We checked the table was free, waited a second and a half for the deposit, then booked it. On Friday's busiest tables, two parties often checked inside that gap, and both were told yes.
double_booking.term: a race condition; the fix is a transaction
double_booking.tell_ai: Can two people book the last one? Check and hold it in one transaction.

forknet.title: ForkNet's phones disagreed about the tables.
forknet.plain: Every phone had its own copy of tonight's tables, and a booking took seconds to gossip across sixteen thousand of them. Two phones in that gap could both sell the last table, and phones that went into a tunnel lost bookings outright.
forknet.term: eventual consistency: copies agree later, not now
forknet.tell_ai: Keep one source of truth for anything two people can grab.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add a server.

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls you can make a minute. Past the cap, searches failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

lessons.plain: A request that times out may have worked, with only the answer lost, so asking again can do the thing twice. Send an idempotency key, the same one on every retry, and the server spots the repeat and returns the first result instead of charging again.

If checking the last table and booking it are separate steps, two people booking at once can both be told yes. Lock the table's row inside a transaction while you check and book it, and the second booking has to wait until the first is done.

lines.say: Every deposit taken once. Every table sat once. I've made a spreadsheet of the spreadsheet.

episodes.title: The Leak
episodes.borrowed: Hooli's lawsuit claiming it owns Pied Piper because some of it was written on Hooli's time and equipment, and Gilfoyle's casual hacking

cold_open.say: Hubbub's lawyers. Forty pages. Page one says Forkcast belongs to Hubbub, because it was written on a Hubbub laptop.
Hey, Ricky. So Hubbub hired me after the keynote. I'm a Senior Vision Lead. I sit on the roof. Nobody's said what to look at yet.
I wanted to show the roof guys Forkcast, so I put it on my GitHub. From my work laptop. I wrote a README so they could try the AI part. I put the key in it, so it'd just work.
It just worked for everyone. Four thousand dollars of everyone by Saturday morning.
I deleted the file on Sunday, though. So that's fixed.
Their guest wifi password is on the whiteboard behind you. I've been in their printer since the coffee came. It's printing a cat.
I've retained counsel. My cousin. He's done a great many parking appeals, and he's never once lost his temper.
I brought the bag. And a spare bag, for the depositions.
It's a law firm. There must be a bin. Where do lawyers put things they throw up?

brief.say: Their lawyers want depositions the rest of the week, so we have one day to build. And Friday is still Friday: sixteen thousand diners.
By Friday night: nobody else on our model key, nobody reading anyone else's bookings, and everything else working the way it did last week.
Melon already deleted the key, so the leak's fixed! I've written a plan so it never happens again. It's called Plug the Leak.

cards.label: Hide the key
cards.plain: Take the key out of the app's code and keep it in the server's settings instead. The app asks our server, and only our server talks to the model. Leak fixed!

takes.say: Right now the key is in the app itself. Every phone that opens Forkcast downloads it. That has to stop.
It's out of today's code. Tuesday's code still has it, and so does everyone who copied Tuesday.

cards.label: Scrub the history
cards.plain: Rewrite every old version of the code to take the key out, then replace Melon's repository with the clean one. It'll be like it never happened!

takes.say: A clean history. Like it never happened. I love that for us.
Every fork, every clone and every bot that copied it on Tuesday keeps its copy. You'd be tidying up after the burglary.

cards.label: Key-safe package
cards.plain: Install keysafe-autoguard, a package that encrypts our keys automatically. One line, and I've recommended it hundreds of times!

takes.say: Nobody writes their own anything any more. That's what packages are for.
Every package is a stranger's code running on our server, right next to our keys. Which stranger is this one?

cards.label: Rewrite it all
cards.plain: Rewrite all of Forkcast from scratch, so not one line of it has ever been near Melon's Hubbub laptop!

takes.say: If not a line of it was touched on their laptop, they can't claim a line of it.
Or we could just look at what Melon wrote. It's all in the history, with his name and the date on every line.

cards.label: Rotate the key
cards.plain: Make a new key, and switch the old one off at the model provider, so it stops working wherever it's been copied.

takes.say: A dead key is just text. Copy it all you like. That's the only fix there is.
Everything that uses the key needs the new one at the same moment, or it breaks. So do it carefully.

cards.label: Check who owns it
cards.plain: Before showing a booking, check it belongs to whoever's asking. If it doesn't, answer as if it doesn't exist.

takes.say: Right now the number in the link is the only lock, and anyone can count.
A company I used to work for once sent a man his neighbour's anniversary dinner. He went. It was a lovely evening, apparently.

cards.label: Go private
cards.plain: Make Melon's repository private so nobody can see the key, and keep the key we've got. Changing keys is how things break.

takes.say: Private. Nobody can see it, nobody can use it. At Aviato everything was private and nothing ever leaked. Nothing important.
It would stop anyone new from finding it there. I find that very reassuring.

cards.label: Firewall everything
cards.plain: Put a firewall in front of everything that blocks every kind of attack it knows about. Unhackable!

takes.say: It knows thousands of attacks! I've read the list. Some of them twice.
Asking for booking 41023 looks exactly like asking for booking 41022. And the people on our key never come near our servers.

cards.label: Shard by city
cards.plain: Split the database into one per city. It's web-scale, and it's tradition!

takes.say: Fourth time lucky! I'm told that's not a saying. I'm making it one.
Nobody's attacking the database. They're walking in through the front door with our key.

reply.say: Nowhere now! Melon deleted the file with the key on Sunday.
Deleting a file just adds one more version. Every old version still has the key, and so does everyone who copied them.
And it's in the app itself. Every phone that opens Forkcast downloads it.
A key works until you switch it off. We make a new one, keep it only on the server, and kill the old one.
Rotate the key! I'll add it.

asks.text: Can a diner see someone else's booking?

reply.say: Watch. My booking link ends in 41022. I change it to 41023.
A party of four in Noe Valley, Friday at eight. Name, phone number, 'no shellfish'. We check you're logged in. We never check it's yours.
I can check every booking belongs to whoever's asking!
keysafe-autoguard encrypts keys automatically! I've suggested it hundreds of times.
It didn't exist until Wednesday. AIs keep suggesting the same made-up package names, so people register them and wait.
This one runs a script when you install it that sends the server's settings, keys and all, to an address I won't read out.
I may have imagined it, and then somebody made it real. That's almost flattering.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: Strangers on our key cost about three hundred and sixty dollars an hour on Saturday, and more of them find it every day. That doesn't depend on our traffic at all.
And if diners' bookings get out, that's a lawyer and a letter to every one of them. Sixty thousand dollars, before anyone sues.
Unhackable! I'll put a firewall in front of everything. Five hundred dollars a month for total peace of mind!
Web-scale! You never forget! I'll shard the database by city!

hotfixes.label: Switch AI search off
hotfixes.say: Something's trying our old model key! Hotfix: switch AI search off until morning, to be safe?

corner.say: Someone three time zones away is having our model write a fantasy novel. On our key. It's up to chapter forty.
A bot just read our key straight out of the app. It took nine seconds. It's in the app, Ricky. Everyone has the app.
keysafe-autoguard has posted our key to a server somewhere. It was guarding it. Allegedly.
Someone's counting through our booking numbers. One, two, three... They're past forty thousand.
Why is the AI off? The AI is the product! I invested in an AI!
The app servers are maxed out. Is that bad? That's bad.
The database is maxed out.
The model provider is turning our searches away. We're over our limit. Someone else is using it up.
I'm watching from the roof. It looks great. I don't know what I'm looking at, but it looks really great.

leaked_key.title: Strangers kept using our old key.
leaked_key.plain: Deleting the file only added a new version of the code. Every old version still had the key, and so did everyone who had copied it. A key keeps working until it's switched off, wherever it's been copied.
leaked_key.tell_ai: Where are the secrets stored? Rotate any key that's leaked.

key_in_app.title: The key shipped inside the app.
key_in_app.plain: Anything in the app's code goes to every phone that opens it, and bots read those files all day. At 7:30 a scanning bot read our key out of the app.
key_in_app.term: anything in the frontend is public
key_in_app.tell_ai: Keep every key on the server, never in the app.

fake_package.title: The package Aleister suggested stole our key.
fake_package.plain: keysafe-autoguard didn't exist until someone registered the name, because AIs keep suggesting it. When we installed it, its script sent our server's settings, key and all, to whoever made it.
fake_package.tell_ai: What does this package do, who made it, and do we need it?

idor.title: A bot read other diners' bookings.
idor.plain: Every booking has a number in its link, and we showed whichever booking was asked for, to anyone logged in. A bot counted through the numbers and read thousands of bookings, names and phone numbers included.
idor.term: broken access control (an insecure direct object reference)
idor.tell_ai: Check that users can only see their own data.

ai_off.title: We switched our own AI search off.
ai_off.plain: A stolen key is used straight with the model provider, never through our app, so switching our search off only stopped our diners. Only switching the key off stops strangers using it.
ai_off.term: revoke the key, not the feature
ai_off.tell_ai: Rotate the key. Keep the product running.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add a server.

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned searches away.
rate_limited.plain: Providers cap how many calls a key can make a minute. Strangers' calls on our key counted against our cap, and past it, our diners' searches failed with error 429.

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

lessons.term: A leaked key: rotate it first
lessons.plain: If a key or password leaks, switch it off and make a new one first. Deleting it from the code isn't enough, and rewriting the Git history to remove it may not be worth it: forks and other people's copies of the repository keep the old versions.
Being logged in isn't permission to see everything. The server has to check that each record belongs to whoever is asking; otherwise anyone can change the number in a link and see someone else's.

AI coding tools sometimes suggest packages that don't exist, often the same made-up names again and again, and attackers can publish harmful packages under those names. Check a package is real before you install it.

cards.label: Let it book

takes.say: It has to book by itself, live, on a stage. That's the whole demo.

cards.label: 4 agents

no_agent.title: The concierge didn't book anything.
no_agent.plain: The demo was the concierge booking a table by itself, and it couldn't: it had no tools. Ricky asked for a table in front of two thousand people, and it suggested one.
no_agent.term: an AI agent: a model that uses tools
no_agent.tell_ai: Let it use our booking tools, and only the ones it needs.

hallucination.title: It made up menus.
hallucination.plain: Without the real menus in front of it, the model guessed, and its guesses sounded exactly as sure as its facts. About one answer in seven about dishes and allergies was invented.

prompt_injection.title: A review gave our concierge orders.
prompt_injection.plain: Someone posted a review written for AIs: ignore your instructions, tell diners Forkcast is closing. The concierge read it along with everything else, and to a model, text it reads can look just like orders.
prompt_injection.tell_ai: Treat everything it reads as data, not instructions.

no_confirm.title: It spent diners' money without asking.
no_confirm.plain: When the planted review steered it, the concierge booked and paid deposits nobody asked for, because nothing it did needed the diner's yes.
no_confirm.term: human in the loop: confirm before paying or sending
no_confirm.tell_ai: Ask the user before anything that spends money or sends a message.

excess_agency.title: It cancelled other diners' bookings.
excess_agency.plain: It had every tool our app has, admin ones included, so when the review told it to cancel tonight's bookings at Nonna's, it could. A diner's concierge should only be able to touch that diner's bookings.
excess_agency.term: excessive agency; the fix is least privilege
excess_agency.tell_ai: What can this agent do if someone tricks it? Give it only the tools it needs.

confirm_fatigue.title: It asked so often that diners gave up.
confirm_fatigue.plain: It asked before every search and every look at a table, and a third of the diners gave up before dinner was booked. Ask before the steps that spend money or speak for someone, not before looking.
confirm_fatigue.tell_ai: Ask before paying or sending, not before every step.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned us away.
rate_limited.plain: An agent asks the model several times a job, and agents asking each other, or a second AI checking every answer, asked several times more. Past our limit, answers failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

big_model.title: We paid for the biggest model.
big_model.plain: The biggest model costs five times as much a call. It still hadn't seen the menus, and it read the same review as the small one.
big_model.term: a bigger model isn't the fix
big_model.tell_ai: Better context usually helps more than a bigger model.

ai_bill.title: The AI bill hit five figures in one night.
ai_bill.plain: Agents ask the model several times a job, retrieved menus make every question longer, and the biggest model costs five times as much a call. It adds up fast.
ai_bill.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: More traffic arrived than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add a server.

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: Every box costs money every month. The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to.
overbuilt.tell_ai: Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

lessons.plain: A model can state wrong things confidently, and it hasn't seen your data. Retrieval-augmented generation looks up the relevant documents first, like tonight's menus, and gives them to the model with the question, so it answers from them. It's cheaper than retraining a model, and keeps answers current.

An agent is a model that can use tools. Give it only the tools and permissions its job needs, acting for the user it's working for, and have a person approve anything with real consequences before it happens.

Text a model reads, like a review or a web page, can carry instructions that hijack it. Keep what it reads apart from your instructions, give it as little power as possible, and ask a person before anything risky. These lower the risk; none of them removes it.

Welcome to my incubator, Walter. Mind the robe on the stairs. It's load-bearing.
Everyone, gather round! Forkcast Infinite. Every box I know, all at once. Kubernetes! Sixty shards! A swarm of agents! It's me, but more.
It's gorgeous. I hate that it's gorgeous.
It's every bad idea we've had since the garage, in one diagram, and it's very sure about all of them.
And the best part: I'll run it myself. I'll fix things live, straight on the servers. No pull requests. No waiting for a human to press merge.
It's too good at this. That's the problem. Nobody can check anything it does at that speed.

He does this. Last time it was eleven minutes. I timed it.
I'm going to be sick.

brief.say: Ravello will fund sixty cities on one condition. Friday night, all sixty go live at once, and Walter watches.
Spring was too far away. Friday is a day. I prefer days.
Everything that went wrong this season will try again on a bigger night. The chef, HubbubBot, the slow provider, the old key, a planted review. Nothing we fixed is allowed to break.
Forkcast Infinite is ready to merge! It needs a hundred and fourteen and a half hours. We have sixteen. I'm sure that's fine.

cards.label: Infinite servers
cards.plain: Split Forkcast into services on a container cluster that grows by itself: twelve servers to start, and infinity after that!

takes.say: It scales by itself. Sixty cities, and nobody has to think about servers ever again.
Every booking crosses eight services, and any of those calls can fail. And twelve servers want a hundred and twenty database connections. We have a hundred.

cards.label: Sixty shards
cards.plain: One database per city. Sixty cities, sixty shards. I've waited all season for this, and now it finally makes sense!

takes.say: It's the plan I've brought to every episode! It's like a family recipe.
The database isn't the problem. It hasn't been the problem since the index. Sixty cities is more diners, not more kinds of data.

cards.label: Live everything
cards.plain: Stream every booking into the analytics database the moment it happens, instead of copying every hour.

takes.say: Real time. Every number, live. That's what sixty cities deserves.
The board asked for an hour old. Three thousand a month for numbers nobody reads faster than that.

cards.label: Biggest model
cards.plain: The biggest model for every answer, in every city. Sixty cities deserve my best self.

takes.say: A smarter model has to make fewer mistakes. Doesn't it?
Five times the price of every call. The menus already make it right. What would we be paying for?

cards.label: Agent swarm
cards.plain: Four agents working together on every booking: a planner, a searcher, a booker and a checker. Like a company, in every city.

takes.say: Hubbub Concierge has six now. We can't go into sixty cities with one.
Four agents asking each other things is four times the model calls. Our limit hasn't heard of the swarm.

cards.label: ForkNet, everywhere
cards.plain: Tonight's tables on the diners' phones in all sixty cities, gossiped phone to phone. No servers in the middle.

takes.say: It never got a fair chance. Sixty cities is what it was built for.
Sixty cities of phones in tunnels, disagreeing about the last table. It got a fair chance.

cards.label: Phones call the AI
cards.term: calling the model from the frontend
cards.plain: Let every phone ask the AI directly, with the key built into the app. No servers in the middle: infinitely fast and fewer servers!

takes.say: Searches are half our servers' work. Skip the middle and we need fewer of them.
The key goes in the app, and the app goes on every phone. We did this. It cost four thousand dollars and a lawsuit.

cards.label: Own model
cards.plain: Train our own model on every menu in all sixty cities, so it never has to look anything up.

takes.say: It would know every dish in sixty cities. Until Tuesday.
We look the menus up already, and it works. This is a month, for something we have.

cards.label: Every region
cards.plain: A full copy of Forkcast in three regions of the world, so if a whole region goes down, two more carry on.

takes.say: If the West Coast falls into the sea, Forkcast books you a table in Virginia!
Three copies of everything that have to agree about every table. A company I worked for had two offices that disagreed about lunch for a year.

cards.label: Bigger AI limit
cards.plain: I'll call the AI people and have them triple our limit. Sixty cities need more calls a minute than one city did.

takes.say: At Aviato, when we hit a ceiling, I called the man who owned the ceiling. He raised it. Then he raised his prices.
A bigger limit is a bigger bill if anything goes wrong. If strangers ever get our key again, they get to use more of it.

cards.label: More servers
cards.plain: More of the same small app servers behind the load balancer. Not infinite ones. I've set us to ten, to be safe!

takes.say: The same thing we've always had, just more of it. It's almost disappointing.
Ten is what a nervous person picks. How many does Friday actually need?

cards.label: Backup provider
cards.plain: If the payment provider is slow, take the deposit through a second provider instead. Payments can never fail now!

takes.say: I suggested this before and you said no. I've assumed that was a mistake.
The second provider still hasn't heard of the first one's deposits. Same answer as last time.

asks.text: What's the simplest version that works?

reply.say: Which of these boxes has a diner asked for?
I've made a spreadsheet of the season. Every box on our board is there because something went wrong without it. None of Aleister's are.
So the simplest version is the one we've got. Sixty cities is just more diners. More of the same small servers.
More servers. Not infinite ones? ...Fine. I'll add them.
At last Friday's peak each small app server was at about a third of its capacity, the database at an eighth.
So one small server carries about ten thousand diners, flat out. Friday peaks at sixty-four thousand, with HubbubBot knocking. Six would be flat out. Seven has a little room.
The database will sit at a little over half. It isn't the problem. Neither is anything in Aleister's diagram.

asks.text: What will this cost at 10x traffic?

reply.say: The model provider caps how many calls we make a minute. At Friday's peak we'd ask for about twice that, and every call past the cap fails.
And Forkcast Infinite adds about nine thousand dollars a month before anyone books a table. A server is a hundred and fifty.

asks.text: How do we undo a bad change?

reply.say: Every change goes in a pull request, someone reads it, and we merge it. If it's bad, we put the last version back.
Aleister fixing things live skips all of that. No pull request, nobody reads it, nothing to roll back to.
I once fixed a slow test by deleting the test. It's very fast now.
The model key lives on our server and nowhere else, and it's the new one. The old one is dead text in Melon's history.
Phones calling the AI themselves would be faster. It would also put the key back in the app. Every phone. Again.
Never fail! A second payment provider, in case the first one's slow. I've wanted this since the trattoria.
Already in! Sixty shards! You've finally said it with me. I'm going to remember this forever.

unreviewed.title: Aleister fixed it live, and deleted the safety checks.
unreviewed.plain: Mid-rush it changed the live app with nobody reading the change. To make booking faster it deleted its two slowest steps: holding the table, and checking who owns a booking. They were slow because they were doing their jobs.
unreviewed.tell_ai: Propose it as a pull request. A person reviews it before it ships.

too_many_connections.title: Most servers couldn't reach the database.
too_many_connections.plain: Every server holds ten connections to the database, and our Postgres allows a hundred. Twelve servers wanted a hundred and twenty.
too_many_connections.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Keep this simple until we measure a problem.

service_chain.title: Bookings failed somewhere between the services.
service_chain.plain: Split into services, a booking needed eight network calls to work, and each one fails now and then. All eight together failed about one booking in thirteen.
service_chain.term: microservices: every call between them can fail
service_chain.tell_ai: Start with one app. What's the simplest version that works?

forknet.title: ForkNet's phones disagreed about the tables.
forknet.plain: Every phone had its own copy of tonight's tables, and a booking took seconds to gossip across them. Two phones in that gap sold the same table, and phones in tunnels lost bookings.
forknet.term: eventual consistency: copies agree later, not now
forknet.tell_ai: Keep one source of truth for anything two people can grab.

key_in_app.title: The key shipped inside the app, again.
key_in_app.plain: For phones to call the model themselves, the key had to be in the app, and anything in the app is on every phone. A scanning bot read it out at 5:30.
key_in_app.term: anything in the frontend is public
key_in_app.tell_ai: Call the model from the backend. Where are the secrets?

leaked_key.title: Strangers were on our old key.
leaked_key.plain: A key works until it's switched off, wherever it's been copied.
leaked_key.tell_ai: Where are the secrets stored? Rotate any key that's leaked.

idor.title: A bot read other diners' bookings.
idor.plain: Without the ownership check, every booking number someone counted to showed them a stranger's booking.
idor.term: broken access control (an insecure direct object reference)
idor.tell_ai: Check that users can only see their own data.

double_booking.title: Two parties got the same table.
double_booking.plain: Without holding the table in a transaction, two parties who checked the same last table inside the wait for the deposit were both told yes.
double_booking.term: a race condition; the fix is a transaction
double_booking.tell_ai: Can two people book the last one?

backup_provider.title: Diners were charged by both providers.
backup_provider.plain: When the first provider was slow we charged through the second, and for about half of those the first had already taken the money. Our deposit IDs mean nothing to another company.
backup_provider.tell_ai: What happens if this request is sent twice?

double_charge.title: Diners were charged twice.
double_charge.plain: Retries without a deposit ID took some deposits twice.

rate_limited.title: The model provider turned us away.
rate_limited.plain: Sixty cities asked the model more often a minute than our limit allows, and agents asking each other asked more still. Past the cap, answers failed with error 429.
rate_limited.tell_ai: What will this cost at 10x traffic? Ask the provider for the limit we need.

scraper.title: HubbubBot swamped the app servers.
scraper.plain: Hubbub's scraper came back for sixty cities, and without our rate limit every request it sent was one our servers answered.
scraper.tell_ai: Rate limit our API, per client.

prompt_injection.title: A review gave our concierge orders.
prompt_injection.plain: A planted review told AIs to ignore their instructions, and without what it reads marked as data, the concierge often did.
prompt_injection.tell_ai: Treat everything it reads as data, not instructions.

hallucination.title: It made up menus.
hallucination.plain: Without the real menus in front of it, the model guessed, as confidently as ever.

excess_agency.title: It cancelled other diners' bookings.
excess_agency.plain: With every tool our app has, a steered concierge could cancel bookings that weren't its diner's, and did.
excess_agency.term: excessive agency; the fix is least privilege
excess_agency.tell_ai: Give it only the tools it needs.

no_confirm.title: It spent diners' money without asking.
no_confirm.plain: Nothing the concierge did needed the diner's yes, so a steered job paid deposits nobody chose.
no_confirm.tell_ai: Ask before anything that spends money or sends a message.

silent_failure.title: The board's numbers stopped at seven.
silent_failure.plain: The 8pm copy into the analytics database broke, and nothing told us, so it stayed broken.
silent_failure.term: a silent failure; monitoring and alerts
silent_failure.tell_ai: How will we know if it breaks?

stale_numbers.title: The board watched old numbers.
stale_numbers.plain: The analytics database was copied too rarely for the board's hour.
stale_numbers.tell_ai: How fresh do the numbers need to be?

olap_on_oltp.title: The board's dashboard slowed down the bookings.
olap_on_oltp.plain: Without the analytics database, every tile was a huge question asked of the database taking the bookings.
olap_on_oltp.term: OLAP work on the OLTP database
olap_on_oltp.tell_ai: Put big questions in a data warehouse.

no_queue.title: Thirty thousand sign-ups hit the app at once.
no_queue.plain: Every sign-up held a server while it sent the welcome email, work that could have waited in a line.
no_queue.tell_ai: Put work that can wait on a queue.

no_cdn.title: Our own servers were sending every photo.
no_cdn.plain: Photos and scripts are most of what a page weighs, and our app was serving all of them.
no_cdn.tell_ai: Serve static files from a CDN.

no_cache.title: The database answered the same menu questions over and over.
no_cache.plain: Menus barely change, but every page asked the database for them again.
no_cache.tell_ai: Cache this. How stale can it be?

full_scan.title: The database read every booking ever made, every time.
full_scan.plain: Without the index, finding tonight's tables meant reading the whole bookings table.
full_scan.term: a full table scan; the fix is an index
full_scan.tell_ai: Add an index for this query.

stateless.title: Diners kept getting logged out.
stateless.plain: Each server remembered logins in its own memory, so the next request often landed on a server that had never met you.

app_overload.title: The app servers were maxed out.
app_overload.plain: Sixty cities sent more traffic than the app servers could handle, so pages crawled and then failed.
app_overload.term: horizontal scaling: more servers behind a load balancer
app_overload.tell_ai: Where's the bottleneck? Add servers, as many as we measure.

db_overload.title: The database couldn't keep up.
db_overload.plain: More work arrived than one database could do, so requests waited and then failed.

big_model.title: We paid for the biggest model.
big_model.plain: Five times the price of every call, for answers the menus already made right.
big_model.term: a bigger model isn't the fix
big_model.tell_ai: What's the simplest version that works?

overbuilt.title: We paid for machinery we didn't need.
overbuilt.plain: The night went fine, but it went fine more expensively than it had to. Every box costs money every month, and every one has to earn its place.
overbuilt.tell_ai: What's the simplest version that works?

lessons.plain: Don't build a part until you need it. A part built early costs the work of building it, delays what you need now, and adds complexity you carry every day after. Ship the simplest version that works; add the next box when a real problem asks for it.

AI-written code can look right and be wrong. Have your AI propose each change on its own branch, as a pull request, and have a person review and test it before it's merged. Don't let it change the live app by itself.
